FOREWORD
T
he Office of the Controller of the Budget is established under Article 228 of the Constitution of
Kenya and enacted by the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, to oversee the implementation of
budgets for the national and county governments by authorising withdrawals from public funds,
as established under Articles 204, 206 and 207 and reporting to each House of Parliament on the bud-
get’s performance, quarterly.
Article 228(6) of the Constitution requires my office to submit to each House of Parliament a report on
the implementation of the budgets of the national and county governments. In this regard, I present the
annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2025/26, covering the peri-
od from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. The report contains cumulative amounts from the beginning of the
financial year in line with Section 9(5) of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429.
The report provides an assessment of the implementation of the approved National Government budget
for FY 2025/26 and the performance of funds received into the Consolidated Fund; exchequer issues
to Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs); Consolidated Fund Services (CFS); and the Equita-
ble Share of revenue disbursed to county governments. It examines how the allocated resources were
spent on development and recurrent programmes, sub-programmes, and projects. Spending is further
disaggregated into economic activities for both development and recurrent votes. Consolidated Fund
Services includes payments on public debt on both interest and principal amounts, pensions and gra-
tuities, salary and allowances for Constitutional Office Holders, and Miscellaneous Services. The re-
port also presents monitoring and evaluation exercise findings carried out by my office for nineteen (19)
Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) in line with section 5(b) of the CoB Act, CAP 429.
The data used in preparing this report was obtained from the approved budget and government statis-
tical data annexed to the budget for FY 2025/26, financial and non-financial budget data submitted by
Ministries, Departments, and Agencies which is further supported by data from the Integrated Financial
Management Information System (IFMIS) and the report for the Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) as
submitted by the National Treasury and monitoring and evaluation findings. The report identifies key im-
plementation challenges and emerging issues that require intervention by the Legislature, policy mak-
ers and implementing entities. In addition, the report provides recommendations to improve budget
execution by enhancing budget absorption and fiscal discipline, and by accelerating the national gov-
ernment’s implementation of development projects.
The findings presented in the report show the importance of strong public financial management sys-
tems in enhancing efficiency, accountability, transparency, and value for money in the utilisation of pub-
lic resources when delivering services. My office remains committed to supporting budget oversight
through the timely approval of withdrawals from public funds, timely reporting, and constructive en-
gagement with Parliament, the National Treasury, Accounting Officers, Development Partners, and the
public.

4.2.2 Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector
The approved budget allocation to ARUD in FY 2025/26 amounted to Kshs.82.41 billion, revised to
Kshs.117.41 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.117.41 billion in Supplementary Budget II,
compared to Kshs.81.43 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 2 per cent of the
gross national budget of Kshs.5.52 trillion and 4 per cent of the MDAs’ budget of Kshs.2.93 trillion. The
allocation included Kshs.72.02 billion (61 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.45.39 billion (39

sion had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.6.11 billion (5 per cent of the ARUD Sector allocation).
The high allocation to the State Department for Agriculture is due to its vital role in Agricultural Policy
and Research Management, National Food Policy, Strategic Food Reserves, Crop Development, Phy-
tosanitary Services, International Compliance, Agricultural Farmers’ Training, and Agricultural Land Re-
source Inventory Management.

7. CONCLUSION
The National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2025/26 aimed to assess the
performance of revenue, exchequer releases, expenditure by Ministries, Departments and Agencies
(MDAs), and the Consolidated Fund Services (CFS), as well as programmes and projects implementa-
tion, in line with Article 228 of the Constitution and in line with Section 5(b) of the Controller of Budget
Act, Cap 429. The assessment provided an important basis for determining the extent to which the ap-
proved budget was implemented and the effectiveness of public resource utilization through the Mon-
itoring and Evaluation Exercise performed in FY 2025/26 for some selected nineteen State Agencies
under six MDAs. The report also identified key issues hampering effective implementation, along with
recommendations.
Overall, budget implementation during the financial year demonstrated resilience amid fiscal con-
straints, competing expenditure priorities, and the need to maintain fiscal discipline. Total receipts into
the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.4.61 trillion, recording 94 per cent of the annual target, while total
exchequer issues to MDAs, Consolidated Fund Services and Equitable Shareable revenue to County
governments were Kshs.4.58 trillion, representing 94 per cent of the annual net estimates.
Total expenditure for the National Government was Kshs.4.75 trillion, accounting for 90 per cent of the
gross budget. Further review demonstrated that recurrent expenditure continued to account for a sig-
nificant proportion of total National Government expenditure, particularly expenditure relating to Con-
solidated Fund Services, recording Kshs.1.98 trillion, and ministerial recurrent expenditure recording
Kshs.1.98 trillion, against ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.809.47 billion. While these ex-
penditures are necessary for the continued functioning of Government, the relatively high recurrent ex-
penditure placed pressure on the resources available for development programmes. Therefore, there
is a need to strengthen expenditure prioritisation in line with the government’s fiscal policy over the
medium term.
The report identified the key issues that hampered budget implementation in FY 2025/26 and need to
be addressed. They include the delay in the adoption of the Electronic Government Procurement Sys-
tem, accumulation of Trade Payables/Pending Bills, use of Article 223 of the Constitution to access Ex-
chequer Issues, Public Debt Management challenges, delay in the implementation of the Equalisation
Fund, delayed disbursement of exchequer funds to MDAs and County Governments and disconnect on
year-end closing procedures and guidelines.
Other key findings identified during the Monitoring and Evaluation exercise performed included: Inade-
quate budget for ongoing contractual obligations; Commencement of projects without approved bud-
gets; Weak reporting mechanisms on Development Partner projects with A-i-A arrangements; Failure to
utilize the Public Investment Management System software to manage projects; and inadequate budget
for associated costs such as utility relocation and compulsory land acquisitions.
Fast-tracking the implementation of the EGPS will improve efficiency and transparency in government
procurement of goods and services; therefore, there is a need to build the capacity of both government
officers and suppliers to use it. The management of Trade Payables/Pending bills remains an important
concern in ensuring sustainable budget implementation. MDAs are required to make sufficient budget-
ary provision to settle eligible pending bills.

The review also underscores the importance of compliance with the Constitution and the Public Finance
Management Act when incurring expenditure under Article 223 of the Constitution that was unforeseen
and/or of an emergency nature. Further to the observations made on public debt management, the Na-
tional Treasury should strengthen and operationalise debt-reduction strategies by accelerating fiscal
consolidation to progressively reduce the fiscal deficit and ensure that the annual debt-to-GDP target
of 55 per cent is attained in the medium term.
The recommendations also emphasised the timely utilisation of the Equalisation Fund for marginalised
counties to provide public services, and the timely release of exchequer issues to Ministries, Depart-
ments and Agencies and Counties to enable the timely implementation of planned activities. To resolve
the year-end cut-off disconnect, public entities should strictly comply with the existing statutory year-
end cut-off requirements while recognising liabilities in accordance with the IPSAS accrual framework,
strengthening commitment management and enhancing transparency in financial reporting
Further, the National Government should continue to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation while
maintaining a predictable and sustainable fiscal framework to reduce the budget deficit. Expenditure
should be aligned with available resources and focused on high-priority programmes with the greatest
potential to support economic growth, employment creation, social protection and improved delivery
of public services.
The National Government should also ensure adequate budget for ongoing contractual obligations,
commence projects only when they have approved budgets, strengthen reporting mechanisms on De-
velopment Partner projects with AIA arrangements, utilize the PIMS software to manage projects and
ensure adequate budget for costs associated with each project such as utility relocation and land ac-
quisition.
The Controller of Budget remains committed to strengthening oversight, promoting fiscal responsibility
and enhancing accountability in the management of public resources. It is expected that the lessons
arising from the monitoring and evaluation exercise in the FY 2025/26 budget will inform improved bud-
get execution, enhanced service delivery, and better socio-economic outcomes for the country.
